title: Why I Stopped Approving My Team's Time Off
author: Karol Wójciszko
summary: Karol Wójciszko argues that engineering managers should stop acting as permission gates for routine time off, early finishes and late starts. Every approval, he says, teaches capable adults that their own judgment is not enough and turns the manager into someone monitoring hours rather than outcomes. He adds that people sometimes keep asking because approval transfers part of the accountability to the manager, a mechanism he compares to code review where two sign-offs mean nobody fully owns the change. The deal is harder, not softer: stop watching hours and judge output only. He says managers must make expectations explicit first, including that projects cannot stall, handovers are documented and open loops are closed. He acknowledges company policy may force formal requests and concludes that an ownership posture can be held within any structure.
points: Routing small requests through a manager signals that people need a blessing to run their own day and makes the manager a bottleneck.
Approval quietly transfers accountability, so the manager ends up holding responsibility that should sit with the person.
Removing the permission step raises the bar because output becomes the only thing left to evaluate.
Freedom comes with explicit expectations: no stalled projects, documented handovers and closed open loops before time away.
Even where policy requires sign-off, a manager can hold an ownership mindset, and the real test is how rarely people feel they need to ask.
quotes: Asking for approval and being responsible are not the same skill, and every time you reward the first one, you’re training your team out of the second.
stop watching hours, start watching output only. If the work gets done and nothing breaks, the day is theirs to shape.
Removing the permission step doesn’t lower your bar, it raises it, because output becomes the only thing left for you to evaluate someone on.
The moment you approve something, part of the accountability moves from them to you, whether you wanted it or not.
Approval doesn’t just grant access. It quietly launders accountability, and as the manager, you’re usually the one left holding what got laundered.
Stop asking where they are. Make sure their absence never becomes someone else’s emergency.
The best test of whether your team actually has ownership isn’t how quickly you approve their requests. It’s how rarely they think they need to ask you at all.
Ownership isn’t a permission structure you get to install, it’s a posture you can hold as a manager regardless of which structure you’re stuck inside.
